newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees signs of power struggle in Baghdad.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees signs of power struggle in Baghdad.

text.p: Senior U.S. officials on Wednesday branded Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein a "demon" and said there were signs of a power struggle in Baghdad.

Reinforcing suggestions of instability in Iraq reported on Tuesday by a senior U.S. military source, White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry offered a terse but carefully worded assessment of the political situation in Baghdad.

"There are a great deal of complicated internal struggles for power" going on, McCurry said in response to questions on that earlier report. It had claimed Saddam had put his wife under house arrest and was changing locations more frequently out of apparent fear for his safety.
"There have been some things that have happened there recently ... (some) that have been reported publicly that would indicate some internal machinations," McCurry said.

A senior military officer called reporters to his Pentagon office on Tuesday to say that various sources he considered reliable reported signs of increasing trouble surrounding Saddam, a bitter foe of the United States since U.S.-led forces ousted Iraqi invaders from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.

Besides the reported house arrest of Saddam's wife, the military officer, who asked not to be identified, said Saddam was now moving around even more frequently than he usually does in order to ensure his own safety.
He also said the Iraqi ruler's eldest son and heir apparent, Uday, might lose a leg to gangrene as a result of a December 12 grenade and machine-gun attack in Baghdad.
Against that background, McCurry said on Wednesday that Washington was "closely monitoring" the situation in Iraq.

"The president (Bill Clinton) also has foremost on his mind the threats to regional security, particularly in the Persian Gulf," McCurry said, noting there were no indications of a renewed threat to Kuwait.

Officials at the State Department, breaking with the usual diplomatic nicities, said Washington was not trying to cast Saddam in an evil light. "We don't need to demonise him," said spokesman Nick Burns. "He is a demon, and he's done it to himself."

Claiming the Iraqi leader breached terms of the peace accord that ended the Gulf War, ignored the human rights of his own people and "lets kids starve because he builds palaces to himself," Burns said "We haven't demonised him. He has become something quite dark in the landscape of the Middle East."

Burns acknowledged the comments on Saddam were co-ordinated. "The U.S. government has a unified position -- Pentagon, State Department, White House, other agencies of the U.S. government -- on Saddam Hussein," he said.
Saddam has been a thorn in the side of U.S. policymakers, who assumed the harsh economic sanctions imposed since the Gulf War would have long since undermined his ability to remain in power.
